opening.headline: When results deteriorate, we explore which part of the plan, tool selection, tool execution, or final answer is at fault, and learn how to fix it appropriately at that specific point.
body: After the change, the success rate dropped, and the logs show multiple failed executions with different reasons. It's unclear whether to modify the prompt, the tool description, or the tool code. Fixing it without understanding the root cause might cause failures elsewhere.

In this class, we learn how to categorize failures into four types: planning error, tool selection error, tool execution error, and answer error. We trace the execution flow from top to bottom to identify the first point of divergence, aggregate errors by type to detect regressions, and verify the reasons for different correction points based on their locations.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Failure can be categorized into planning, tool selection, tool execution, and final answer.
It is possible to determine whether the modification point is valid.

screens.title: Don't know where to make the changes since the results have worsened.
screens.lead: First, let's examine a common situation many teams encounter. Read the following scenario and think about what might be blocking progress.

visual.alt: Below the graph showing declining success rate, multiple execution records failing for different reasons are displayed, with a branching path prompting which area to fix.

paragraphs: After the recent change, the agent's success rate dropped. Upon reviewing the logs, multiple failed executions were found. Some incorrectly defined steps, others invoked different tools, and some had invalid date formats. Each case has a distinct cause.

In this state, it's difficult to determine what needs to be changed. It's unclear whether to modify the prompt, the tool description, or the tool code. And without understanding the root cause, making changes to one area might inadvertently cause another area to fail again.

Therefore, failure should not be labeled simply as "wrong," but rather with a tag indicating where it occurred. This is the question we will address in this class: when we categorize failure by the location where it occurs, what changes?

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Could changing the prompt resolve the input validation issue with the tool's code? I'll return to answer this question when the class ends.

screens.outro: First, let me recall how I record failures.

screens.title: Have you ever broken down failures by root cause?
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't enter or submit your answer, so think for yourself first and then click.

items.prompt: Didn't you simply record recent failures as "just wrong"?
items.answer: It tells you that a mistake has occurred, but does not indicate where to make the correction. Even when the issue is described as a "mistake," the location of the fix differs between a misalignment in the plan and a faulty tool factor. Labeling the item is the starting point of any correction.

items.prompt: Have you ever distinguished whether a failure was due to the plan or the tool?
items.answer: If you don't distinguish between different failure types, all failures may seem to stem from prompt issues. However, failures arising from overlapping tool descriptions or loose tool input validation do not disappear even if you modify the prompt repeatedly.

items.prompt: Have you ever counted the occurrences of failures stemming from the same root cause?
items.answer: When categorized by cause, several types account for most failures. Addressing the more common types yields the greatest impact with the same effort. The aggregation method used in this course helps with that task.

screens.outro: I've organized my thoughts, so now I'll verify the four possible locations of failure.

screens.title: Four locations of failure: planning, tool selection, tool execution, response
screens.lead: Select each tab to examine the four locations where failures occur and their respective characteristics. On the last tab, you can verify the classification rules.

tabs.label: Plan error
tabs.body: This is a failure due to a misalignment in the plan—caused by incorrectly understanding the user's intent or omitting necessary steps. A typical example is assuming conditions that the user did not state and thereby constructing inappropriate steps. If the plan itself is wrong, even perfectly accurate tool calls later will result in the wrong actions.

tabs.label: Tool selection error
tabs.body: Failing to call the appropriate tool for a given situation or failing to call a required tool. Anthropic explains that agents may incorrectly call the wrong tool or fail to make a required call. For example, calling a general FAQ tool instead of an order lookup tool in a customer refund inquiry.

tabs.label: Tool execution error
tabs.body: The tool was chosen correctly, but this is a failure due to incorrect parameters or tool error. It is a case where the correct tool is used with incorrect parameters. For example, passing a date in the format 3/5 instead of the required format. Since the tool selection is correct, it must be distinguished from a selection error.

tabs.label: Response error
tabs.body: A failure occurs when the tool results are misinterpreted or stated without evidence, resulting in an incorrect final sentence. For example, when the tool returns a total of 42,000 won, but the response incorrectly states 24,000 won. As Anthropic points out, agents can also mishandle tool responses.

tabs.label: Classification rules
tabs.body: Attach one location per failure. The criterion is the first location among the four that is misaligned. If an earlier step is incorrect, errors in subsequent steps are merely consequences thereof and are not counted separately. This ensures that a single failure is not redundantly aggregated across multiple categories.

screens.outro: Now that we know the location, let's follow through the process of classifying the actual ten failed cases.

screens.title: Classify 10 failure cases into four types
screens.lead: Follow the process of grouping the 10 hypothetical failure cases by type. Select the right arrow to review each group sequentially.

visual.alt: A bar graph divided into 10 failures, 3 planned, 3 tool selection, 2 tool execution, and 2 responses.

steps.title: Examples 1~3: Planning Errors
steps.body: Three cases involve assuming conditions that the user did not state, leading to incorrect steps. Since the plan is already misaligned with the goal before even considering how the tool was invoked, these are classified as planning errors.

steps.title: Cases 4~6: Tool Selection Errors
steps.body: Three cases regarding refund inquiries instead of order lookup used the general FAQ tool instead of the order verification tool. The intention was correctly to verify the order, but the wrong tool was selected to execute that plan.

steps.title: Case 7~8: Tool Execution Error
steps.body: Two cases where the wrong tool receives an argument with an incorrect date format. The tool selection is correct, so this is not a selection error but an execution error.

steps.title: Example 9~10: Answer Error
steps.body: The tool results are correct except for two cases where numbers were misplaced in the final sentence. The first three steps are all correct, and the first error occurred in the final sentence.

steps.title: Aggregation and Priority
steps.body: Aggregated, there are three planning items, three tool selection items, two tool execution items, and two response items. The two types with the highest counts are the top candidates for correction. The classification results indicate the priority for modification and provide direction on which locations to fix.

screens.outro: After classifying, we will now look at how to find the first line that diverges in the actual trace.

screens.title: Read the trace line to locate the failure position
screens.lead: The following are three hypothetical traces. You can see why a line failed by selecting the highlighted line. Read from top to bottom and locate the first mismatched line.

data.text:
[trace A]
plan: After order inquiry, refund notification
tool_call: search_faq(q="refund")
answer: Refund is possible

[trace B]
plan: Refund guidance after order verification
tool_call: get_order(date="3/5")
tool_result: error, date must be YYYY-MM-DD
answer: Currently, verification is difficult

[trace C]
plan: Total order amount guidance
tool_call: get_order(id="A17")
tool_result: total=42,000
answer: The total amount is 24,000 won.

marks.span: plan: After order inquiry, refund notification
marks.note: This is the plan for trace A. The plan to check the order and then provide a refund is correct. Therefore, the first line is not inconsistent, and reading should continue to the next line.

The plan is order inquiry, but a general FAQ tool was invoked. Initially seeming misaligned, the plan is correct while the tool is different, indicating a tool selection error. The following response shows the result of this selection.

The tool is correct, but the argument does not match the required date format. Therefore, an error occurs on the very next line. This is a tool execution error because the tool is correct but the argument is wrong.

marks.span: tool_result: error, date must be YYYY-MM-DD
marks.note: This is the error returned by the tool. As an error message indicating the correct format, the agent must be able to use this information to retry. The agent's decision to stop at "the last response was unclear" is merely a consequence of a previous execution failure.

marks.span: answer: The total amount is 24,000 won.
marks.note: The tool result matches total=42,000, but the numerical value was incorrectly moved in the final sentence. All previous lines are correct, and the error first appears at the end, so this is an answer error.

screens.outro: Now that we've learned how to find locations, let's see how this classification is used in regression detection.

screens.title: Regression detection: what is visible when traced by type
screens.lead: When moving the slider to monitor regression, verify what information, when viewed together, makes the root cause more apparent.

stops.body: While we can see that there is regression based on overall success rate, we cannot determine where the regression originated. We are unable to distinguish whether it stems from poor planning or poor tool invocation, thus unable to identify the exact area requiring correction.

By categorizing failures into four types and comparing the counts before and after the change, we can identify the types that have increased. For example, if only tool execution errors have increased, this change might be related to tool inputs.

Anthropic recommends collecting not only accuracy but also execution time of tool calls, total number of tool calls, token usage, and tool errors. If duplicate calls are common, consider questioning the response size or page settings; if parameter errors are frequent, consider questioning the tool descriptions or examples.

By including failed cases in the evaluation set under the same type of evaluation criteria, you can immediately identify recurrence when failures reoccur. This goes beyond simply knowing the location, evolving into a system that prevents issues from reappearing after being fixed.

screens.outro: Now that we know the detection method, let's examine how modifications vary depending on location through examples.

screens.title: Explanation: Tool selection errors and tool execution errors are different in terms of where they need to be fixed.
screens.lead: The instructor explains a hypothetical case step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: The two errors appear similar.
steps.body: Both errors appear superficially to be due to incorrect tool invocation. However, the first error arises because the wrong tool was invoked, while the second error occurs because the wrong argument was passed to the correct tool. The treatment differs depending on the location of the root cause.

steps.title: Causes of Tool Selection Error
steps.body: The descriptions of two similar tools overlap, causing the agent to become confused. Anthropic explains that agents struggle to determine which tool to use when tools overlap or their purposes are ambiguous. Having too many tools or overlapping tools also hinders the development of efficient strategies.

steps.title: Correction for Tool Selection Error
steps.body: Clarify tool descriptions and refine naming conventions. By prefixing service or resource names with a prefix, boundaries become clearer. Consolidate tools that have overlapping functionalities. There is no need to modify the tool codes here.

steps.title: Causes of Tool Execution Errors
steps.body: The tool selected the right option, but the parameter format is incorrect or the error response is unhelpful, preventing the agent from retrying. For example, a date is incorrectly formatted from YYYY-MM-DD to 3/5. When there are many parameter errors, it signals the need for clearer explanations or examples within the tool.

steps.title: Fixing Errors in Tool Execution
steps.body: Enforce the input model so that error messages provide correct input examples. Anthropic recommends providing specific, actionable improvements rather than opaque error codes or trace details. This time, the change is made on the tool side, not the prompt.

steps.title: Conclusion: The type determines the modification point.
steps.body: No matter how carefully the tool descriptions are refined, the parameter format issues remain unresolved, and strengthening input validation does not eliminate overlapping tool descriptions. Since fixing one aspect does not resolve the other, determining the failure location is equivalent to identifying the point of correction.

screens.outro: Finally, I will summarize the method for determining whether a modification is valid.

screens.title: Explanation: Determining whether the amendment is valid
screens.lead: When an item is selected, the instructor's explanation is displayed. Review each item one by one and check what needs to be verified after making modifications.

items.prompt: Has the number of failures for the modified type decreased?
items.answer: The first thing to verify is the number of incidents of the issue type that I have fixed. If the tool execution error has been resolved, the count of that issue type should decrease. If the count remains unchanged, it means either the wrong location was fixed or the fix has no effect.

items.prompt: Didn't other types of claims increase as well?
items.answer: Fixing one place might cause another to break. If changing the tool description leads to more tool selection errors, then the modification has created a new problem. Compare all four types of counts before and after the change to verify rollback.

items.prompt: Can evaluation criteria containing the same failure be passed?
items.answer: If a failure is reclassified as a validation criterion, then after fixing it, retest that criterion. If it passes, the failure is now resolved and will be monitored as a regression test in the future.

items.prompt: Has the number of tool calls and token usage been improved?
items.answer: Success rates can be the same yet efficiency can differ. By examining the number of tool calls, token usage, and tool error counts together, you can verify whether the correction has progressed to the actual execution phase. A reduction in duplicate calls indicates that the response size settings have been appropriately adjusted.

items.prompt: How do you know the modification point is wrong?
items.answer: If you fixed the wrong location, the number of failures of that type remains unchanged. This indicates a misjudgment of the failure location, so go back to the trace to locate the original erroneous line again.

screens.outro: I will conclude by summarizing the contents so far.

screens.title: The failure location determines the fix point.
screens.lead: Let's revisit the initial question by reflecting on the flow of the lesson.

paragraphs: Failure is divided into four categories: plan, tool selection, tool execution, and answer location. Tracing is read from top to bottom, and a label is attached at the first point of deviation. By aggregating and comparing pre- and post-change states according to type, we can identify where regression occurred.

Changing the prompt does not resolve the tool input validation issue. It determines the location of the modification point. After correction, verify whether the type has decreased or whether another type has not increased.

glossary.def: Failure occurs when the intent is misinterpreted or when necessary steps are omitted, causing the plan itself to become misaligned.
Failing to call the appropriate tool for the situation or failing to call for a required tool.
The correct tool was selected, but the failure occurs due to incorrect parameters or tool error.
This is a failure to misinterpret tool results or to arrive at a final answer without proper justification.
This involves initially dividing and aggregating failures by their respective locations where they first occur, and then determining the correction points.

misconceptions.myth: Failure is always a prompt issue.
misconceptions.fact: The places that need to be fixed vary. Many failures are resolved by modifying tool descriptions, tool codes, error messages, or response instructions.

misconceptions.myth: Tool selection errors and tool execution errors are addressed using the same remedy.
misconceptions.fact: Selection errors are resolved through tool documentation organization and naming conventions, while execution errors are addressed through input validation and improved error responses. One does not resolve the other.

misconceptions.myth: Looking at the overall success rate is sufficient.
misconceptions.fact: The overall success rate only indicates that degradation has occurred. To determine where the degradation happened, aggregation must be performed by type.

closing.lead: This summarizes the core content covered in this course.
points: Dividing failure into planned elements, tool selection, tool execution, and four positions of response reveals the root cause.
Comparing aggregate results before and after changing the type can help detect regressions.
Tool selection errors and tool execution errors have different correction points.
Verify the location of the failure against the patch point, and confirm that no new types have emerged after the patch.
closing.reflectionLead: Finally, here's a question for you to think about on your own. Please feel free to recall it at your convenience—no submission or grading is required.
closing.reflection: What is one recent failure of mine that I could place among your five positions, and what would be the first clue to verify at that location?

checks.q: Pair up the failure cases with their corresponding failure locations.
left: Assumed conditions not stated by the user led to an incorrect sequence of steps.
Instead of checking order status, they called the general FAQ tool for refund inquiries.
Passed an invalid argument with incorrect date format to the right tool
The tool results are correct, but the numerical value was misplaced in the final sentence.
checks.explain: Failure classification is assigned based on the first point of divergence among planning, tool selection, tool execution, or response.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Some pairs do not match. Re-examine where the first misaligned position is.

What is the failure point and appropriate correction point in the following trace?  
plan: After order confirmation, send refund notice  
tool_call: get_order(date="3/5")  
tool_result: error, date must be YYYY-MM-DD  
answer: It is currently difficult to verify
options: This is a plan error, so the user intent understanding guideline is corrected.
Tool selection error; therefore, tool descriptions and naming conventions are being clarified.
Due to tool execution errors, input validation is strictly enforced and appropriate examples are included in the error messages.
Since this is an answer error, additional guidance on numerical verification of the final sentence is provided.
checks.explain: The plan and tool selection are correct; the initial misalignment was due to a wrong parameter format in the function call. Tool execution errors are resolved through input validation and improved error responses.

wrong.0: The plan is correct, so it did not initially deviate.
wrong.1: Since the appropriate tool was selected, a prescription for selection error does not apply.
wrong.3: The response is merely a result of a previous execution failure.
